variants.name: Private final fields with accessors and defensive copies
variants.idiom_name: private final fields assigned in the constructor + accessor methods
variants.implementation_notes: Assign the fields once in the constructor, expose read access only through accessor methods and never hand the fields out: `final` makes every later assignment - from the class's own methods or from a subclass - a compile-time error, and a private field is invisible to subclasses altogether. Because `final` constrains only the reference, mutable arguments must be copied in the constructor with `List.copyOf`/`Map.copyOf`/`Set.copyOf` (Java 10+) or the `Collections.unmodifiable*` wrappers, and the accessors must return those unmodifiable copies rather than the fields. Keep the separate Data class for the case where several fields form one invariant validated and frozen as a unit, or where the holder is shared with another object.
pitfalls: A `final` field protects the reference, not the object: `final List<Item> items` still allows `items.add(...)`, so copy with `List.copyOf` or expose unmodifiable views.
Removing setters and the no-argument constructor breaks JavaBeans-based frameworks (JPA, bean serializers); they fail at runtime or fall back to reflection.
Reflection and `Field.setAccessible` still write final fields - modern JDKs warn about it - so the pattern protects against accidents, not against hostile code.

variants.name: Record as the language-level data carrier
variants.implementation_notes: A record is the pattern built into the language: the compiler generates one private final field per component plus a public accessor of the same name, the class is implicitly final (so no subclass can exist to write the state) and `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString` come for free. Add a compact canonical constructor to validate the components and defensively copy mutable ones, since the generated field is final but the object it references need not be immutable. Choose records for pure data carriers fixed at construction; keep a plain class with accessors when behaviour, inheritance or a framework contract requires it.
pitfalls: The generated accessors return the stored references: mutable components must be copied in the canonical constructor or callers can mutate the 'immutable' record.
Records are final and cannot extend or be extended, so a hierarchy that wants to share read-only state through a superclass cannot use them.
Serialization deserializes through the canonical constructor, so validation runs - but `writeObject`/`readObject` hooks are not available, and non-serializable component types fail at runtime.
